description_full: Becton, Dickinson and Company develops, manufactures, and sells medical supplies, devices, laboratory equipment, and diagnostic products for healthcare institutions, physicians, clinical laboratories, reference laboratories, pharmaceutical industry, and the general public worldwide. It operates through Medical Essentials, Connected Care, BioPharma Systems, and Interventional segments. The company provides peripheral intravenous (IV) and advanced peripheral catheters, central lines, acute dialysis catheters, vascular access technology, vascular care and preparation products, needle-free IV connectors and extensions sets, closed-system drug transfer devices, hazardous drug detections, hypodermic syringes and needles, anesthesia needles and trays, enteral syringes, and sharps disposal systems; IV medication safety and infusion therapy delivery systems, medication compounding workflow system, automated medication dispensing and supply management systems, informatics and analytics and pharmacy automation system, and medication inventory optimization and tracking system; hemodynamic monitoring system; and prefillable drug delivery systems. It also provides hernia and soft tissue repair, synthetic mesh, biological and bioresorbable graft, biosurgery, and other surgical products; surgical infection prevention, peripheral intervention, and urology and critical care products; as well as peripheral vascular and endovascular technologies, including angioplasty balloons, stents and stent graft, vascular access, drainage and biopsy devices, dialysis access solutions, vessel closure and arteriovenous fistula creation and maintenance technologies, inferior vena cava filters, atherectomy, thrombectomy, and ablation platforms. The company was founded in 1897 and is headquartered in Franklin Lakes, New Jersey.

financial_summary: Becton, Dickinson and Company is a large-cap healthcare business with a $59.5B market cap on $19.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +0% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 5% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 47%.

The business throws off $2.9B in free cash flow — roughly 15 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.15× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.5× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.0×.

Management returns a meaningful 6.0% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 12% operating margin runs 12pp above the Healthcare median (0%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.32x).
It accounts for 0.4% of sector revenue and 0.6% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-17.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 466 companies in the universe; the top four hold 35% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 31% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 2% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 26% and a beta of 0.53, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $315.3M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 30% in the 2020 crash, 20% in the 2022 bear market and 34% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 25% below its DCF fair value of $291, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 41%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $127 to $620 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Healthcare peers: P/E 43.4 vs 26.6 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 16% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.9% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 14 covering analysts target $226 on average, 3% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 5% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.81).
It runs a 47% gross margin and converts 15% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 3.15x.
ROE of 5% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.1x equity multiplier).
It spends 5.1% of revenue on R&D and 1.3% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.5x net debt to EBITDA ($725.0M of cash against $16.3B of debt), with interest covered 4.0x.
The current ratio of 0.87 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
Goodwill makes up 51% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 0.1% over 3 years, -0.8% over 5 years and 4.5% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -3.0% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.3x depreciation (3.5% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 13, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 3.2% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.4%), and institutions hold 99%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (8 sales, net $1.9M sold).
It returns 6.0% a year to shareholders (4.1% in buybacks and 1.9% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.0% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 43 consecutive years, raising it 2.1% a year over the last five.
people: With about 62,000 employees, each generates about $314K of revenue, 0.8x the Healthcare median, and revenue has grown 6.1% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $47K of free cash flow per employee.
